title: Huberman Lab × Robert Greene — 焦虑是思考的引擎
title_en: Huberman Lab × Robert Greene — Anxiety as the engine of thought

questions.question: Robert Greene 认为，阻碍一个人把别人的观点变成「活的想法」的主要是什么？
options: 外部干扰：工作和社交占用了时间，没有足够的独处来思考
焦虑：没有安全感的人会抓住第一个能让焦虑消失的答案，不再往下翻转
信息不足：读过的书和资料还不够多，手里就没有足够多的不同观点可供比较
智力限制：只有少数人天生具备把观点推到反面的思维能力
questions.explanation: Greene 说焦虑是在提醒你还有东西没弄懂；能忍住焦虑的人会继续想「也许是 A，也许是 B」，忍不住的人就停在第一个答案上。
questions.question_en: According to Robert Greene, what mainly keeps someone from turning others' ideas into "living ideas" of their own?
options_en: Outside distractions: work and social life eat the solitude needed to think
Anxiety: insecure people grab the first answer that makes the anxiety go away and stop turning the idea over
Too little information: without enough books and sources, there aren't enough views to compare
Intellectual limits: only a few people are born able to push an idea to its opposite
questions.explanation_en: Greene says anxiety signals that you don't yet understand something. Those who can tolerate it keep going, "maybe A, maybe B"; those who can't stop at the first answer.

questions.question: Greene 借 Hofstadter「坐直升机到珠峰顶」的比喻谈 ChatGPT，他担心的是？
options: AI 很快会取代作家这类职业，写作者会因此失去生计
AI 生成的答案常常不准确，直接拿来用会让人得出错误的结论
跳过了焦虑与挣扎的过程，思考的「肌肉」就长不出来，看到的风景一样却不是同一个时刻
一切工具都会让人退化，所以应当像他自己一样拒绝使用搜索引擎
questions.explanation: 他并不反对工具，自己天天用 Google；他担心的是顺序反了、人被工具用。Huberman 补的那句是：走过的路会改变你到达的地方。
questions.question_en: Borrowing Hofstadter's image of "taking a helicopter to the top of Everest," what worries Greene about ChatGPT?
options_en: AI will soon replace professions like writing, and writers will lose their livelihoods
AI answers are often inaccurate, so using them directly leads people to wrong conclusions
Skip the anxious struggle and the thinking "muscle" never grows; the view is the same, but it isn't the same moment
All tools make people degenerate, so one should refuse even search engines, as he does himself
questions.explanation_en: He isn't against tools; he uses Google daily. His worry is the order getting reversed, the tool using the person. Huberman adds: the journey transforms where you arrive.

questions.question: Greene 说把视频调成静音、只看对方的身体，就能看穿对方是否真诚。节目页的说法核查怎么判断这一说法？
options: 有据但说宽了：静音观察确实更准，只是效果没有他说的那么大
与证据相反：人辨别谎言的平均正确率只有 54%，而且听声音比看画面判得更准
无法核查：相关研究都在实验室里进行，无法用来评估这种说法
证据充分：元分析显示，经过仔细观察肢体语言，人辨别谎言的准确率甚至可以超过八成
questions.explanation: Bond 和 DePaulo 的元分析显示平均正确率 54%，且听声音比看画面更准，静音恰好丢掉了更有用的线索。核查也注明了限度：没回答训练能否改变结果。
questions.question_en: Greene says that by muting a video and watching only someone's body, you can tell whether they're sincere. How does the episode page's claim check rate this?
options_en: Supported but overstated: watching with the sound off is more accurate, just less dramatically than he says
Contrary to evidence: people detect lies only about 54% of the time, and do better listening than watching
Unverifiable: the studies were all done in labs and can't be used to assess the claim
Well supported: a meta-analysis shows that by reading body language, accuracy can exceed eighty percent
questions.explanation_en: Bond and DePaulo's meta-analysis found 54% average accuracy, with audio beating video, so muting throws away the more useful cues. The check also notes its limit: it doesn't say whether training changes the result.
